results.result: Monkey S, a 7-year-old female Rhesus macaque, initially showed normal behavior and successfully completed basic training protocols at a comparable rate to control monkeys.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 provide consistent demographic and behavioral data showing that monkey S initially appeared behaviorally normal and completed basic training protocols (transport box and primate chair familiarization) at rates comparable to controls. These observational data are internally consistent and provide baseline characterization of the subject.

results.result: Monkey S showed severely impaired performance on visual task training, requiring substantially longer times to complete fewer trials than control monkeys and failing to progress beyond initial training stages across multiple task paradigms.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C13 and C15 provide quantitative performance metrics across multiple visual tasks showing consistent impairment: prolonged trial completion times (30-103 min vs. 18-25 min expected), inability to progress to higher task complexity, and high error rates (23-51 errors per session). The consistency across different tasks and training paradigms strongly supports the conclusion of severe visual task impairment.

results.result: Despite severe impairment on formal visual tasks, monkey S showed preserved basic visual orienting abilities in naturalistic settings, though with some atypical behaviors including abnormal eye fixation patterns and reaching strategies.
results.evaluation: Claims C14, C16, and C18 provide observational data showing preserved gross visual abilities (orienting to objects and rewards, normal locomotion in home cage) alongside atypical behaviors (sideways reaching while running). Claim C17 acknowledges a limitation (no quantitative eye tracking). The dissociation between preserved naturalistic vision and impaired task performance is well-documented.

results.result: Structural MRI revealed an almost complete bilateral loss of primary visual cortex (V1) in monkey S, likely congenital or perinatal in origin, with expected bilateral visual field loss affecting central and peripheral vision.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C21 and C23 provide converging evidence from structural MRI, clinical assessment, and retinotopic mapping. The imaging clearly shows the lesion (C19), clinical evaluation rules out acquired injury (C21), and the visual field loss estimation (C23) is based on established retinotopic maps with appropriate citations. The inference of congenital/perinatal origin is reasonable given the lack of injury history and preserved subcortical structures.

results.result: The lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) in monkey S showed no reduction in size compared to controls, with volumes of 47.0 mm³ and 48.5 mm³ (left and right) versus control mean of 50.0±4.7 mm³ and 51.5±5.1 mm³, suggesting absence of retrograde degeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C29 provide quantitative volumetric data showing LGN volumes in monkey S fall within the control range. The comparison with cited literature (C24, C25) showing LGN atrophy in adult-acquired V1 lesions strengthens the interpretation that the preserved LGN structure indicates early developmental timing of the lesion. The measurements are appropriately quantified with standard deviations.

results.result: The superior colliculus (SC) and pulvinar showed comparable volumes in monkey S and control monkeys, with no evidence of atrophy.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31 provide quantitative volumetric measurements showing SC and pulvinar volumes in monkey S fall within control ranges. The data are appropriately quantified with means and standard deviations, supporting the conclusion of preserved subcortical visual structure.

results.result: Post-mortem high-resolution imaging revealed that V1 cortex in monkey S was substantially thinner (0.9-1.3 mm) than controls (1.4-1.8 mm) with the stripe of Gennari positioned closer to the pial surface, suggesting particular reduction of superficial layers, while extrastriate area V5/MT showed normal thickness (1.9-2.0 mm).
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C38 provide detailed quantitative measurements from high-resolution post-mortem imaging. The observations of altered stripe of Gennari position (C32-C33) and quantitative thickness measurements (C35-C36) support the inference about superficial layer reduction (C34). The preserved V5/MT thickness (C37-C38) provides important contrast. The measurements are specific and internally consistent.

results.result: In vivo myelin-weighted imaging showed that area V5/MT in monkey S exhibited normal myelination patterns and surface area (86.9 mm² left, 78.8 mm² right) comparable to published normative data (82.4±8.9 mm²).
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42 provide methodological justification (C39) and quantitative measurements showing V5/MT myelination and surface area in monkey S fall within published normal ranges. The comparison with published data using the same method (C42) strengthens the conclusion. The measurements are appropriately quantified.

results.result: In anesthetized fMRI experiments with visual stimulation, the LGN showed significant activation (z>2.3) to flickering checkerboards in monkey S and three control monkeys, while cortical activation was less consistent across controls and minimal in monkey S, and pulvinar was not consistently activated by checkerboards.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C48 describe the experimental design, inclusion criteria, and results showing robust LGN activation in monkey S comparable to controls, but reduced cortical activation. The use of an objective threshold (z>2.3) and restriction to animals meeting this criterion (C44-C45) strengthens the analysis. The variability in cortical responses is acknowledged (C47, C52), which is appropriate given the methodological challenges.

results.result: The strong LGN activation in monkey S to checkerboard stimulation was equivalent to controls and suggests that visual information from the retina can reach the brain, indicating an intact visual pathway prior to V1.
results.evaluation: Claims C49, C50, C51, and C116 provide converging evidence from functional activation data showing robust LGN responses in monkey S comparable to controls. The inference that this indicates intact retinal input to LGN (C49, C116) is reasonable and consistent with the structural findings of preserved LGN (C26-C29). The reduced cortical activation (C51) is expected given the V1 lesion.

results.result: Moving dot stimuli produced lower activation levels than checkerboards across all animals, with monkey S showing some LGN activation (left hemisphere) and pulvinar activation, plus sparse cortical activation in dorsal STS near V5/MT.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59 and C117 provide consistent quantitative data showing reduced activation to moving dots compared to checkerboards across all subjects. The observation that LGN activation to moving dots was lower than to checkerboards (C117) is consistent with known LGN cell properties. The spatial distribution of sparse cortical activation is documented (C58). The variability across subjects is appropriately noted.

results.result: Quantitative ROI analysis showed that monkey S had no V1 activation (V1:LGN ratio = 0) compared to control median of 0.83, no significant V5/MT activation to either stimulus, but significant pulvinar activation specifically to moving dots.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C64 provide quantitative ROI-based measurements showing clear differences between monkey S and controls. The absence of V1 activation (C61) is expected given the lesion. The stimulus-specific pulvinar response to moving dots (C63) and comparison with the only control showing pulvinar activation (C64) provide important functional characterization. The measurements are appropriately quantified.

results.result: Detailed spatial analysis revealed multiple small regions of BOLD activation (z>2.3) to moving dots within the STS of monkey S, including areas MST and FST, but mainly outside anatomically defined V5/MT, suggesting sub-threshold activation difficult to detect with BOLD.
results.evaluation: Claims C67 and C122 provide detailed spatial characterization of activation patterns, acknowledging the presence of foci of activation while noting they fall outside the anatomically defined V5/MT ROI. The inference about sub-threshold activation (C122) is reasonable given the methodological limitations discussed elsewhere. The spatial specificity adds important detail to the functional characterization.

results.result: Functional connectivity analysis using V5/MT as a seed region revealed an intact network of bilateral dorsal extrastriate cortex, parietal areas, and frontal eye fields (FEF) in monkey S that was comparable to control monkeys, suggesting preserved inter-cortical connectivity despite V1 loss.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C74, C78, and C123 provide converging evidence from functional connectivity analysis showing preserved cortical networks in monkey S. The bilateral pattern (C70, C74), inclusion of expected regions like FEF (C72, C125), and consistency across subjects (C73, C78) support the conclusion. The inference that inter-cortical connectivity is preserved (C123) is well-supported by the data. The methodology is appropriate for addressing limitations of activation-based analyses.

results.result: Neither LGN nor pulvinar as seed regions produced consistent patterns of cortical connectivity in monkey S or controls, with LGN notably absent from the V5/MT functional network, possibly reflecting weak anatomical connectivity in typical animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C75 and C124 report negative findings from connectivity analyses using subcortical seeds. The absence of LGN in the V5/MT network (C124) is interpreted with reference to known weak anatomical connectivity (cited). These negative results are important for understanding the functional architecture and are appropriately reported with mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: Probabilistic tractography showed that monkey S had identifiable white matter tracts between LGN/pulvinar and V5/MT, but these tracts followed different, less direct routes that appeared to project around the lesion compared to the reasonably consistent tracts in six control monkeys.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 provide comparative tractography results showing altered but present connectivity in monkey S. The observation that tracts take circuitous routes around the lesion (C81) is consistent with the anatomical constraints and suggests developmental plasticity. The comparison with consistent control patterns (C79-C80) provides appropriate context. The qualitative observations are supported by the imaging data shown.

results.result: Quantitative tractography analysis showed that while the microstructure of tracts between V5/MT and subcortical nuclei appeared intact in monkey S (FA values comparable to controls), the number of streamlines reaching target was very low (0.01-0.03%) - at least an order of magnitude lower than controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C86 provide quantitative tractography metrics showing a dissociation between preserved microstructure (FA values) and reduced tract size (streamline counts). The measurements are appropriately quantified and the comparison with controls is clear. The inference that microstructure is intact (C86) is supported by the FA data. This dissociation is important for understanding the nature of the connectivity changes.

results.result: Given the significantly weakened tracts between V5/MT and subcortical nuclei, there is little evidence that strengthening of these connections underlies residual vision in monkey S, though the lack of significant differences in microstructure suggests either or both pathways could support residual visual abilities.
results.evaluation: Claims C87 and C130 provide interpretations of the tractography findings regarding mechanisms of residual vision. The conclusion that strengthened subcortical-V5/MT connections do not underlie residual vision (C87) is supported by the reduced streamline counts (C83-C84). The more cautious interpretation (C130) acknowledging that preserved microstructure could still support function is appropriate. These interpretations are logically consistent with the data.

results.result: fMRI with face stimuli revealed activation of anterior and middle face patches in the ventral STS of monkey S at locations consistent with previous macaque studies, with one control showing only the anterior patch, and no differences between threatening and neutral expressions.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C92 report face patch activation in monkey S. While the locations match published data (C91), the authors explicitly note they did not use the critical control of scrambled faces (C91), which is standard for face patch localization. This missing control makes it uncertain whether the activation is truly face-selective or reflects general visual stimulation. The result requires validation with appropriate controls before conclusions about face processing can be drawn.

results.result: The activation of face patches in temporal cortex of monkey S suggests intact subcortical inputs to temporal visual cortex from pulvinar, claustrum, and amygdala, as these activations must be driven by visual subcortical input other than to V5/MT based on functional specialization.
results.evaluation: Claims C126 and C137 make inferences about subcortical pathways supporting face patch activation. However, this interpretation depends on the face patch activation being valid (C89), which is uncertain due to missing scrambled face controls. The authors appropriately note this needs further scrutiny (C126). The anatomical reasoning is sound, but the conclusion cannot be supported without validating the face-selective nature of the activation.

results.result: Multiple factors complicate interpretation of fMRI results in anesthetized monkeys, including effects of anesthesia type and depth on BOLD activation, individual differences in sulcal anatomy, potential for spurious signal fluctuations, and the bilateral nature of the lesion in monkey S preventing within-subject control comparisons.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C115, C120-C121 provide comprehensive discussion of methodological limitations affecting fMRI interpretation. The challenges are well-documented in cited literature (C110-C111, C113) and appropriately acknowledged. The specific issues with anesthesia effects (C110-C112, C120), anatomical variability (C113), and lack of within-subject controls (C115) are important caveats. The inference that anesthesia suppressed V5/MT activation (C120) is reasonable given the data patterns.

results.result: Based on unremarkable day-to-day behavior, monkey S presumably had reasonable residual vision supported by an intact dorsal visual network with potential to support active vision, though the specific pathways (LGN and/or pulvinar to dorsal areas) remain uncertain due to inconsistent cortical activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C129 and C141 make inferences about residual vision and supporting mechanisms. While the behavioral observations (C127) and intact dorsal network (C128) are supported by data, the specific pathways supporting residual vision (C129) remain speculative. The authors appropriately acknowledge uncertainty due to anesthesia effects on cortical activation. The inference about residual vision is reasonable but the mechanistic explanation requires additional evidence, particularly from awake behavioral studies.

results.result: The source of visual input supporting function in monkey S likely involves parallel, alternative subcortical inputs directly to extrastriate cortex (V2, V3, V4, V5/MT) rather than preserved V1 connectivity, with a wider pattern of weak, parallel subcortical inputs potentially supporting visual awareness and behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C139 present speculative mechanistic explanations for residual vision. While the authors appropriately rule out preserved V1 connectivity (C132) and cite relevant literature on parallel pathways (C134-C136), the proposed mechanism of widespread weak subcortical inputs (C138-C139) is largely speculative. The reasoning is logical and consistent with cited frameworks, but lacks direct empirical support from the current data. This represents a plausible hypothesis requiring future testing rather than a supported conclusion.

results.result: Visual structures outside the V1 lesion remained intact with little atrophy in monkey S, with weak but intact microstructure in subcortical-V5/MT connectivity, suggesting maintenance of structural integrity when V1 is damaged neonatally, which may explain increased residual function compared to adult-acquired lesions.
results.evaluation: Claims C140, C142-C144 provide a synthesis of structural findings and their implications. The preservation of subcortical structures (C140), intact tract microstructure despite reduced size (C142), and contrast with adult-acquired lesions (C143) are all supported by the presented data and cited literature. The inference about timing-dependent effects on structural preservation (C143-C144) is well-supported by comparative data from the literature and the current findings.

results.result: The behavioral presentation of monkey S parallels cortical visual impairment (CVI) in children, who can be misdiagnosed without careful investigation, and imaging was essential for identifying the occipital tissue loss in this case.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 draw appropriate parallels between monkey S and human CVI cases, with proper citation of clinical literature (C93). The observation that imaging was necessary for diagnosis (C94) is clearly supported by the case history showing initially normal-appearing behavior. This comparison provides important translational context for the findings.

results.result: Unlike adult-acquired V1 lesions which show LGN atrophy, monkey S showed preserved LGN structure, consistent with very early (possibly in utero) V1 loss, as preservation of LGN structure and function after V1 lesions depends on age at lesion and lesion extent based on studies in humans and non-human primates.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C102 provide comprehensive literature context showing that LGN preservation in monkey S contrasts with adult-acquired lesions (C95-C99) but is consistent with developmental timing effects documented in marmosets (C101). The inference about very early lesion timing (C102) is well-supported by the structural preservation, cited literature, and clinical assessment (C21). The comparative analysis across species and lesion timing strengthens the interpretation.

results.result: The preserved V5/MT myelination in monkey S could be identified in vivo due to high-resolution scanning and consistent macaque anatomy, and while tract microstructure appeared similar to controls and human hemianopia cases, the bilateral lesions may have caused greater disruption, with reduced tract size possibly reflecting reduced feedback rather than feedforward connectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C108 provide methodological context (C103-C104), comparison with human studies (C105, C107), and mechanistic interpretation of tractography findings (C106, C108). The inference that reduced tract size reflects feedback rather than feedforward changes (C108) is appropriately presented as speculative but is consistent with the preserved FA values. The comparison with human studies strengthens the interpretation while acknowledging differences due to bilateral lesions.

results.result: The pulvinar activation to moving dots in monkey S was as great as the best control subject, consistent with an increased role for this structure in early lesions, while the lack of consistent V5/MT activation in monkey S and some controls suggests anesthesia suppression, contrasting with consistent hMT+ activation in human hemianopia studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C120 provide comparative analysis of pulvinar and V5/MT activation with appropriate citations. The interpretation of enhanced pulvinar role (C118) is supported by cited literature on developmental plasticity. The inference about anesthesia effects (C120) is reasonable given the contrast with human studies (C119) and the variable control data. The integration of current findings with literature provides appropriate context.
